sign_convention.positive_angle: swings a downward-hanging part's tip toward +x (forward)
sign_convention.calf: thigh_angle - knee_flexion (knee bends the heel backward)
sign_convention.forearm: shoulder_angle + elbow_flexion (elbow brings the hand forward)

canonical_rig.T0436_source: @DennieSeth's skeleton reference, zorder_fix_2026-10-08/dennie_canonical_skeleton_ref.png. That file is not present in this worktree or this card's attachments -- every number below is transcribed from the task card's own body/comment (which record it as measured by seeding the image and snapping to the drawn strokes, confirmed by 1px scanline for the two bars), not re-derived from the source pixels by this round. See docs/design/23-canonical-rig.md "Where these numbers came from."

leg_proportions.projection_reasoning: In this lunge the near thigh points away from the viewer (compressed) while the near shin crosses the view plane (full length), so the near-side ratio (1.78) is a projection artifact rather than anatomy; the far-side ratio (1.11) sits inside the anatomical range (1.0-1.1) and is adopted instead. This REVERSES the general near-side-is-truth rule for THIS pose's legs only -- that rule still holds for the arms (upper_limb_reference_comparison below).
leg_proportions.why_not_applied: thigh_R/calf_R (mirrored to thigh_L/calf_L) already drive the leg geometry of every existing animation (walk_cycle, idle_cycle, sitting_idle_cycle); rescaling them to the adopted fractions would shorten every one of those legs by roughly a third, which is exactly the animation re-derivation this card's scope excludes. Recorded here as the target for the follow-on cards that re-derive each animation's own leg geometry.

upper_limb_reference_comparison.note: Upper arm is already close to the reference (within 0.03 of spine, 'already right'); forearm is about +30% over. Neither is corrected this round, for the same reason as leg_proportions.why_not_applied -- every existing animation drives its forearm length from this same rig entry, and rescaling it is the follow-on cards' business.

lateral_offset_axis.description: A per-part, opt-in sideways (local-x) displacement -- rig_compositor.build_placements's lateral_offset_frac parameter, expressed as a fraction of the torso's own width. Distinct from z-order: z decides which part wins a contested pixel, this moves the pixel itself. Every part defaults to 0.0 (no displacement, no behaviour change) unless named in a caller's own dict; no existing pose module (walk_cycle, idle_cycle, sitting_idle_cycle) passes this parameter, so none of them is affected by this axis existing.
lateral_offset_axis.demonstration_values_note: FIX ROUND 2 (docs/design/23-canonical-rig.md Sec 3c): fix round 1 (@DennieSeth, 2026-10-08T21:08) equalized shoulder_L/forearm_L and thigh_L/calf_L to these same values, correctly diagnosing that four DIFFERENT per-part offsets tear a chain apart -- but rig_compositor.build_placements still applied the offset twice per chain (once inherited through forward kinematics from the root, once again explicitly at the distal part's own name), so the equalized dict values still produced a DOUBLED effective shift at forearm_L/calf_L (measured: forearm_L -0.700 x torso vs shoulder_L -0.350 x torso, exactly 2x). The reviewer's FAIL verdict (2026-10-08T21:54:30Z) caught this by direct measurement. This round removes the second, redundant lateral() application in rig_compositor.build_placements -- the offset is now applied exactly once, at each chain's root, and the distal part inherits it purely through FK, so equal dict values now produce an equal effective shift. A consequence: the chain is now rigid and cannot tear at any magnitude, so the real risk is the whole chain detaching from the main body, not a tear partway along it -- re-swept directly against the fixed code (4-connectivity component labelling): the arm chain first detaches a new >=50px fragment at -1.00 (none from -0.10 through -0.95), the leg chain at -0.80 (none from -0.03 through -0.70).
lateral_offset_axis.fix_round_5_note: @DennieSeth's fix-round-5 comment measured the fix-round-2 arm-chain value (-0.35) against the SHOULDER JOINT ITSELF, not just the silhouette: it opens a wedge of background in the armhole (between shoulder_L and torso, within 130px of the shoulder joint) because the sleeve is pushed clear of the torso entirely -- the earlier sweep (fix round 2, above) only checked for NEW detached blobs, never the armhole gap. A uniform part up-scale does not close it: the part is pinned at its own pivot (the proximal/shoulder end), so scaling only extends the DISTAL end further out -- the sleeve-to-torso gap is unaffected by scale, only by this offset. Re-swept directly against the fixed code (with the width-restore anisotropic scale already applied, so these are the actual committed sleeve geometry, not the pre-fix isotropic one): armhole wedge px / sleeve-torso overlap px / (shoulder_L + forearm_L) visible px by offset -- -0.35: 3322 / 166 / 23963, -0.25: 1482 / 1274 / 22824, -0.16: 516 / 2982 / 21096, -0.10: 184 / 4523 / 19580, -0.05: 52 / 5865 / 18231. Chosen: -0.10, bracketed on both sides -- -0.05 leaves only 231px of margin above the 18000px far-arm-visibility floor (too close to the edge the far arm being hidden again), while -0.16 and above reopen the armhole past the 400px ceiling. -0.10 keeps a comfortable margin on both bounds (184px of 400 on the wedge side, 1580px of margin above the 18000px floor on the visibility side) while `shoulder_L` genuinely overlaps the torso (4523px) rather than merely abutting it.
